> @ColinSORourke one thing I'm wondering about as well, but this may be worth a follow up PR, instead of supplying 4 drawable textures to write too, we should also support supplying a texture array of up to 4 layers.

@BastiaanOlij Just making sure I understand correctly, do you mean
A) To change the code at the base, GLSL layer, to support `uniform sampler2D name[4]` instead of 4x `uniform sampler2D`
OR
B) to change the code at the user exposed abstraction to support passing a TextureLayered resource (AKA Texture2DArray) as a parameter instead of TypedArray\<Texture2D\>

Edit: I'll also note that the user exposed abstraction is currently always called from 1 of the output textures in the first place, and accepts up to 3 'other' output textures. So we would either need to perform the operation to merge the 'original' output into the TextureLayered 3 others, or design a new abstraction that can be called independently from any target.

> B) to change the code at the user exposed abstraction to support passing a TextureLayered resource (AKA Texture2DArray) as a parameter instead of TypedArray<Texture2D>

This one, though it's really an edge case we might want to reserve until we have a proper use case for it. I can see there might be some benefits to doing so when manipulating stereo images.

> @RodZill4 , you might want to take a look at this as well, I think this would be very valuable for Material Maker. That would be a good stress test for writing to the 4 textures as I can imagine that generating texture ORMs this way could be nice.

Hmm I moved all Material Maker rendering to compute shaders, and already write to several textures at once (when painting).
I can see a use for this in other projects, though (the VR scene edit one), but will this be forward+ only?

@Bonkahe 

> second are uniforms meant to be unsupported? I tested around with sending custom data to COLOR instead of the blited texture, and one thing I tried was a uniform of source color, and that threw an error.

Yes they are meant to be supported, great catch. I do see the bits of GLSL I'm missing, and am going to get to work on that.

> As an aside, would it be possible to sample the current texture/destination UV we are copying into inside of the blit shader? or is that a no go? I assume it's not possible but I just wanted to be sure.

I can definitely see how that would be helpful, I don't think it would be too difficult, I'll just investigate the best way to surface those values to the user.

@RodZill4 
> but will this be forward+ only?

Learning how to correctly compile Shaders in Forward+ tripped me up a scooch, so I focused on implementing in Compatibility Renderer to get a working implementation sooner. By the end, this feature should be equally available in both Render pipelines.

@beicause 
> I'm bit hard to understand the usage of `DrawableTexture2D.blit_rect_multi`. Why it is needed instead of using 4 drawable textures separately and calling `DrawableTexture2D.blit_rect` on each?

Performance reasons - faster to make a single call to the GPU with 8 textures, than 4 calls to the GPU with 2 textures each. You can still call 4x Blit_Rects individually if you so choose

> Also why does DrawableTexture2D only accept 4 sources instead of using them as material uniforms? Custom uniform textures seem don't work and are always black.

Extra Material Uniforms with textures should work - I'll investigate and fix.

I made my own custom LightOccluders but I need a way to carve out the polygons from the light texture, my current, suboptimal solution is adding the background color on top of the light texture. Personally I disagree with the current design of drawable textures. See also my implemention in #106331.
From my perspective, it needs to be simplified:
1. Input colors could simply be provided via uniforms.
2. Only a single output is necessary.
3. Repeatly drawing seems less essential, as it generally can be worked around.

Regardless, I truly appreciate the effort in this PR, and it was what inspired me to open #106331. However I believe its design requires careful consideration.
After the recent changes it's much better now, but I found another problem - DrawableTexture's `get_image()` returns `null`.

Works correctly now.

2 more things (but they are more up to discussion):
- The DrawableTexture will emit `changed` signal every time it's modified. It _somewhat_ makes sense, but not sure if this is really expected. Texture's `changed` signal is used to e.g. update size of nodes. Modifying DrawableTexture (outside `setup()`) does not modify its size.
I think the `changed` signal should not be emitted when blitting, only when texture's parameters change (size, mipmap count etc.). That's how ViewportTexture behaves btw.

- `blit_rect()` was changed to blend by default, because it's more intuitive. That's true, but blitting and blending are 2 different things I think. Check Image methods for example, it also differentiates them. Hence I originally mentioned `blend_rect()`, which would blend by default, while blit should replace by default IMO.
Looks like Blit shader is not properly supported by VisualShaders. Can't be used at all.

I did a couple tests for performance vs raw compute (raw blitting performance specifically)

Test Project:
[DrawableTextureTests.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21563440/DrawableTextureTests.zip)

Methodology:
For the compute version I setup the compute shader and uniform lists then within the loop I just update the buffer containing the rect data, then execute the compute shader, following this I await the for frame end (to ensure the timers capture the full amount of time required to execute the compute shaders).
For the drawable texture method I used your project as a base and did a couple modifications to make it a bit more 1 to 1 with the compute, namely I make it reference texturerects, and use the textures found within them, as I have to rebuild the textures on the fly for the compute this made sense to keep the number of differences to a minimum.

Possible problems:
Since I am setting up the compute outside of the loop it could be argued it's not an apples to apples comparison, as with the drawable texture execution I'm assuming it's re-setting up the compute shaders each execution, I did it this way mainly because in a real world use case this is the way I would have set it up.

Results:
(time in seconds)

60 iterations:
> Drawable Texture method: Iterations:60 Duration: 0.12599992752075
Compute method: Iterations:60 Duration: 0.00099992752075
 
120:
> Drawable Texture method: Iterations:120 Duration: 0.17799997329712
Compute method: Iterations:120 Duration: 0.00500011444092

2000:
> Drawable Texture method: Iterations:2000 Duration: 3.02600002288818
Compute method: Iterations:2000 Duration: 0.00600004196167

Conclusion:
Obviously compute is significantly faster, though in this situation I doubt anyone would argue that it was ever going to be slower, it's more of a matter of whether it is easier to use, and if you look at the code written for both methods (even including the blitting shader), I doubt anyone can say that the compute implementation is easier to use or to manage lol.

One note, I assume there is some sort of syncing taking place which is the cause of the lower performance with the drawable texture method vs the compute method, so I tried executing with a hold for each frame in the loop and this was the results:

> Drawable Texture method: Iterations:120 Duration: 0.17599987983704
Compute method (wait between each execution): Iterations:120 Duration: 0.99900007247925

Which is significantly slower than the drawable texture method, so I'm not really sure where the disconnect is there, it's certainly not waiting for a frame each execution, so idk, regardless, excellent work, hope this helps with performance diagnostics!

@arkology 

> Maybe there should be a warning if array size is bigger?

You're suggesting a warning like "Passed 5 inputs into Blit_Rect_Multi, only first 4 will be used"? I could see that, but not sure how useful it would be and if it's common in Godot to throw warnings for excess input.

> And "DrawableTexture" completely ignores the "AtlasTexture" region, and this is a big problem for me.

To be clear, you're suggesting a workflow where you set the 'atlas' of an AtlasTexture as a DrawableTexture, like 
```
var myAtlas: AtlasTexture = AtlasTexture.new()
myAtlas.atlas = drawTex
```
And the issue is that if you then call `myAtlas.atlas.blit_rect(rect, source)` , the rect passed in to blit_rect operates from the top left corner of the whole texture, and not the top_left corner of the atlas's current 'region'? I'm unsure how we could codify that behavior in-engine, but you can run some math on rect & region to achieve the desired effect I think. Something like:
```
myAtlas.atlas.blit_rect(Rect2i(myAtlas.region.position + rect.position, rect.size), source)
```

EDIT: I'm realizing you could also mean that DrawTex.blit_rect(rect, AtlasTex) blits the whole AtlasTexture instead of a the AtlasTexture's current region. I'll investigate a fix for that behavior.

> Is it possible to create fully transparent DrawableTextures? Right now it is always white rect.
> It's possible, but you need to draw a fully transparent rect first manually.
> This sounds not very convenient :D
> I am at "small brain mode" at the moment, but looking at DrawableTexture2D docs description as a user, blend_mode will be really useful and frequently-used IMO.

Yeah, to get a transparent DrawableTexture, you have to blit the whole rect with a transparent Source on Blend_Mode_Disabled. Currently the most straightforward code for that would be
```
var myMat = BlitMaterial.new()
myMat.blend_mode = BlitMaterial.BLEND_MODE_DISABLED
drawTex.blit_rect(whole_rect, transparent_texture, Color.WHITE, 0, myMat)
```

We've had conversations about simpler ways to expose other blend modes as easier to write default behaviors, but for various reasons are waiting for more feedback - I appreciate yours, and will keep it in mind

About `AtlasTexture` - try to create `AtlasTexture` resource with some region in your test project and place the path to it into one of load() in test project script. It will draw the whole sprite.
(I haven't looked at how the current implementation works under the hood, so I tested this PR by making a few small changes to the test project, i.e. I worked with this feature as a "beginner user")

AtlasTexture is merely a wrapper for `CanvasItem.draw_texture_region`. Note that the underlying data is still the entire texture.

> But looking at the DrawableTexture2D documentation description as a user, blend_mode will be really useful and frequently-used in my opinion.

I agree that blend mode is commonly used and think it should be implemented as a method parameter rather than a shader mode. Additionally, drawing a full-rect color can be achieved through `clear_color`.

Just push a FINAL set of changes. Patch Notes:
* Changed `DrawableTexture2D.setup` API so the user can specify a base color to initialize the texture to. This will unfortunately error out some of the cool projects built earlier in this thread, but is a pretty easy fix
* Improved SRGB handling - SRGB now appropriately adjusts by output in Blit_Rect_Multi, instead of being all or nothing.
* Changed the 'fallback' texture for blit_sources to white instead of black. This makes it easier to do `Texture.blit_rect(rect, null, modulateColor)` as a simple way to blit a flat color.
* Added Experimental warning to DrawableTexture2D Docs - still highly sensitive to API feedback on those functions.
* Adjusted the Blend_Sub and Blend_Add behaviors - should better match intuition.
* Simplified BlitMaterial to recompile Shader immediately (like SkyMaterials) rather than going through a queuing process
* Rebased on to Master (Sep. 25th)

Great catch @mk56-spn - I investigated today and determined that this is because Blit_Rect overflows RenderingDevice's texture_owner, because every blit_rect call creates new shared textures as the targets for the frame buffers.

No solution yet, but obviously these temporary shared textures need to be freed at some point, rather than building up infinitely. The obvious solution caused my Frame Buffer creation to crash because I freed the Shared before the draw call actually processed - going to keep investigating, will have a fix soon!

Resolved @mk56-spn reported issue in a push just now (12/22). Ran his test case with the fix for 40 minutes at 120fps (so approximately 864k Blit_rect_multi calls), no issues encountered.

Fix, per @clayjohn's suggestion on Rocket Chat, is to pre-generate the slices and store them as part of the DrawableTexture. These are stored in a new Vector<RID> in the TextureStorage::Texture struct, cached_rd_slices, and are initialized as part of Drawable_Texture_initialize. They do not need a separate free process, as they are freed as dependencies of RD_Texture when it is freed.
